sentences.text: Edmontosaurus is classified as a saurolophine hadrosaurid, a group of duck-billed dinosaurs characterized by smaller, solid crests or fleshy combs rather than large hollow ones.
A 2022 study proposed that a fully grown adult Edmontosaurus annectens would measure up to 11 to 12 meters in length and have an average body mass of approximately 5.6 metric tons.
Earlier estimates suggested that fully grown adults could reach lengths of up to 12 meters and average weights of about 5.6 metric tons.
Exceptionally large specimens of Edmontosaurus annectens measured around 15 meters in length and weighed approximately 15.9 metric tons.
Previous estimates indicated that some larger specimens reached 12 to 13 meters with a body mass of about 4 metric tons.
The genus Edmontosaurus was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917.
The type species Edmontosaurus regalis was also named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917.
The species Edmontosaurus annectens was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1892.
In 2025, Tuinstra et al. detected ancient hydroxyproline in an Edmontosaurus fossil, confirming the presence of original organic material.
Edmontosaurus was a herbivore capable of moving on both two and four legs.
Research on Edmontosaurus fossils has revealed details about its brain, feeding methods, and injuries including attacks by tyrannosaurs.
Anatosaurus copei and E. saskatchewanensis are now considered growth stages of E. annectens, with A. copei representing adults and E. saskatchewanensis representing juveniles.
The genus Edmontosaurus includes synonyms such as Anatosaurus, Anatotitan, Claosaurus annectens, and Ugrunaaluk.
The name Anatosaurus is considered a junior synonym of Edmontosaurus because its type species was reassigned to Edmontosaurus.
A previous conception of Edmontosaurus included three valid species: E. regalis, E. annectens, and E. saskatchewanensis.
Edmontosaurus fossils date from the Late Cretaceous, spanning the Campanian to the end of the Maastrichtian.
Fossils of Edmontosaurus regalis are found in western North America and date to approximately 73 million years ago.
Fossils of Edmontosaurus annectens date to approximately 65.5 million years ago.
Edmontosaurus was distributed across western North America, from Colorado to the northern slopes of Alaska.
The assignment of Trachodon selwyni to Edmontosaurus regalis is considered of very doubtful validity by recent reviews.
The proper taxonomy of the A. copei specimens remains a subject of ongoing debate.
A 2017 study questioned the identification of Ugrunaaluk as a separate genus, regarding it as a nomen dubium indistinguishable from other Edmontosaurus.
It is debated whether the larger hadrosaurid Anatotitan copei is a synonym of Edmontosaurus annectens rather than a distinct larger species.
